A person makes a round-trip journey, finishing where she started. What are the displacement and distance for the trip?
column2: Displacement = 0 (net position change is zero). Distance = some nonzero value (total path length still adds up).

column1: True or False: "20 m, west" likely describes the displacement for a motion.
column2: True — it has both magnitude (20 m) and direction (west), matching a vector quantity like displacement.

column1: A person walks A→B→C→D covering legs of 35 yds, 20 yds, and 35 yds. What is the TOTAL DISTANCE?
column2: 90 yds (35 + 20 + 35). Distance sums every leg regardless of direction.

column1: For the same A→B→C→D path, why is stating "the displacement is 50 yds" (with no direction given) incomplete?
column2: The magnitude (50 yds) may be right, but displacement is a vector — without a stated direction, the answer is incomplete/incorrect.

column1: True or False: Velocity is a vector quantity and speed is a scalar quantity.
column2: True.

column1: True or False: Both speed and velocity refer to how fast an object is moving.
column2: True — they both describe rate of motion; velocity additionally includes direction.

column1: Person X travels A→B in 5 s. Person Y travels the same A→B in 10 s. Is Person Y moving at twice the speed of Person X?
column2: False — Person Y took LONGER to cover the same distance, so Y is moving at HALF the speed of Person X, not twice.

column1: True or False: The velocity of an object refers to the rate at which the object's position changes.
column2: True.

column1: True or False: The phrase "30 mi/hr, west" likely refers to a scalar quantity.
column2: False — it includes a direction (west), making it a VECTOR quantity (velocity), not a scalar.

column1: True or False: An object which is slowing down has an acceleration.
column2: True — slowing down is still a change in velocity, and acceleration measures any change in velocity (not just speeding up).

column1: True or False: An object moving at constant speed in a circle has an acceleration.
column2: True — its direction is constantly changing, so its velocity is changing even though its speed isn't. That's still acceleration (centripetal).

column1: True or False: Acceleration is the rate at which the velocity changes.
column2: True.

column1: True or False: An object that is accelerating is moving fast.
column2: False (not necessarily) — accelerating only means velocity is CHANGING. An object can accelerate while moving slowly, momentarily at rest, or even while slowing down.

column1: What formula finds average velocity from displacement and time?
column2: v = d / t (or Δx / t).

column1: What formula finds acceleration from initial and final velocity over a time interval?
column2: a = (v<sub>f</sub> − v<sub>i</sub>) / t

column1: What formula finds final velocity from initial velocity, acceleration, and time (no displacement needed)?
column2: v<sub>f</sub> = v<sub>i</sub> + at

column1: What formula finds displacement from initial velocity, time, and acceleration (no final velocity needed)?
column2: d = v<sub>i</sub>t + ½at²

column1: What formula relates final velocity, initial velocity, acceleration, and displacement WITHOUT time?
column2: v<sub>f</sub>² = v<sub>i</sub>² + 2ad

column1: What formula finds displacement using the average of initial and final velocity times the time interval?
column2: d = ½(v<sub>i</sub> + v<sub>f</sub>)t

column1: Car & Ramp Lab: How do you find instantaneous velocity at a gate, given the wing width and the time the wing blocked the gate's light beam?
column2: v = (wing width) / (time light was blocked) — e.g. 1 cm / 0.0148 s ≈ 67.6 cm/s.

column1: Car & Ramp Lab: Once you have instantaneous velocity at gate A and gate B, how do you find acceleration down the ramp?
column2: a = (v<sub>B</sub> − v<sub>A</sub>) / (time from A to B).

column1: A car drives 500 m in 30 s, then 200 m in 60 s, then 100 m in 120 s. Why is the average velocity NOT just the average of three separate speeds?
column2: Average velocity = TOTAL distance ÷ TOTAL time = (500+200+100)/(30+60+120) ≈ 3.81 m/s — the segments have unequal time, so a simple average of speeds would be wrong.

column1: A ball is thrown straight up at 30 m/s and returns to the same height it was thrown from. What are v<sub>i</sub> and v<sub>f</sub> for the whole flight, and why?
column2: v<sub>i</sub> = +30 m/s, v<sub>f</sub> = -30 m/s — same speed, opposite direction, by the symmetry of motion under constant gravity (a = -9.8 m/s² throughout).
